orientation.signIn: Sign in to take the orientation check.
orientation.title: Your next move starts here.
orientation.intro: Review the lessons, check your understanding, then use the tools with a clear purpose.
orientation.review: Review the process before the check

0.label: A process you can keep using
0.idea: The goal is work you can get and keep. The resume is one part of that process.
0.explanation: Start with what you have actually done. Choose a direction, find a real opening, prepare the right documents, apply, and practice. Overview connects your saved work to a next action. You can return to an earlier step when something changes.
0.example: A new interview invitation changes what matters today. It does not erase your earlier work.

1.label: Your factual foundation
1.idea: One true history can support several directions.
1.explanation: Your starting resume gives you a foundation. Build your Master Draft with work you can explain: what you did, where, when, and what happened. Keep uncertain details as questions to check. A stronger sentence is useful only when it still describes your work.
1.example: “Helped with deliveries” might hide route planning or checking orders. Ask what you actually did before naming those skills.

2.label: Meet your coach
2.idea: t.ROY helps you do the thinking. You keep the final say.
2.explanation: Ask for a screen explanation, help describing your experience, or one question at a time. Check what t.ROY suggests. An AI can misunderstand, miss a detail, or invent one. Never keep a claim just because it sounds confident.
2.example: Try: “Ask me what I did before you rewrite this line.” A suggestion is not a saved change or a sent application.

3.label: Choose work with a reason
3.idea: A real posting gives your preparation a purpose.
3.explanation: Compare the duties and requirements with your experience and practical needs. Separate a requirement from a preference and from something you still need to ask. A keyword overlap is a starting point, not proof you qualify.
3.example: A job may fit your skills but start before the bus runs. Check that constraint before spending time on the application.

4.label: One job, one packet
4.idea: Tailoring changes the emphasis. It never changes the facts.
4.explanation: Choose the actual job and resume version. Bring the relevant work forward, check every suggested line, and inspect the documents you will send. Keep each job’s packet together so you know which version an employer received.
4.example: The same warehouse experience can show order accuracy for one opening and training new coworkers for another, if you really did both.

5.label: Finish the real action
5.idea: Preparing an application and submitting it are different steps.
5.explanation: Read the employer’s instructions. Check the preview and downloaded files. Submit through the employer’s required channel, then record what happened in Applications. Sending a packet to yourself does not apply to the employer.
5.example: Mark Applied after you actually submit. If an interview arrives, update that job so preparation stays attached to it.

6.label: Practice what you can defend
6.idea: You should be able to explain every line in your own words.
6.explanation: Choose the job you are preparing for. Practice a specific example, listen to the follow-up, and look for missing detail. Use feedback to try a clearer answer. A polished script you cannot explain will not help you in a real conversation.
6.example: “I work well under pressure” becomes useful when you can describe a real busy shift, what you did, and what happened.

7.label: Make room for real life
7.idea: A practical hurdle deserves a practical next step.
7.explanation: Use support tools for needs such as transportation, housing or training. Read who a service serves, its source, and what still needs checking. A checked listing does not guarantee eligibility or an available place. Planning what to disclose is your choice.
7.example: For a transport problem, ask about the route and shift time. Do not assume a more confident answer fixes the ride.

8.label: A different direction, the same person
8.idea: Explore without losing the work you already built.
8.explanation: A lane keeps a direction and its documents together. You might explore a trade, freelance work, a creative path, or a CV. Check which lane and job are selected before asking for changes. The underlying history stays consistent.
8.example: A creative portfolio and a job resume may show different parts of your work. Neither needs an invented background.

9.label: Settings is part of the work
9.idea: Make the workspace fit how you read, think, and choose to share.
9.explanation: Settings covers your coach, reading help, motion, contact details, privacy, security, data and usage. These choices affect the whole experience. The separate settings lesson walks through each group and points to the actual controls. Reading a lesson changes no setting.
9.example: Prefer less movement? Choose Reduce motion. Want shorter explanations? Try Plain language. Sharing choices deserve their own careful look.

10.label: Access is different from preparation
10.idea: Opening a tool does not mean the work is finished.
10.explanation: The progress guide recommends an order, while your access and remaining AI allowance determine what you can use. You can ask to open a guided tool early. Support and basic practice stay reachable. Other tool, voice and spending limits still apply.
10.example: Passing the optional check opens guided tailoring and application tools immediately. It does not submit an application, add a paid plan, or remove usage limits.

11.label: Put it into practice
11.idea: You have seen the process. Now choose your next move.
11.explanation: Try the optional six-question check below. Get every answer right to earn immediate guided tool access. There is no timer, no limit on retries, and explanations for anything you miss. You can also leave and come back from Help or Settings.
11.example: This checks your understanding of the tools. It is not a hiring assessment, a credential, or a judgment of your ability.

bands.sub: Every mark comes from the meter's own math, not round numbers. How it works is at the bottom of this page.

how.title: How the meter works
how.units: Each part counts real units of work. The first unit counts the most, every doubling adds the same again, and each part stops adding at its limit. So the fastest way up is to use a part you haven't touched yet, not to repeat one.
how.marks: The marks are worked out from that math: {firstLoop} is your first resume, first tailored resume and first application; {everyPart} is every part started once; {breadth} is every part used past its first steps; {depth} is every part used in depth.
how.nothing: Nothing here looks at speed, logins or time on screen. Going slow doesn't cost you a thing. Removing your own work is your right; the bar just follows what is saved.
how.counts: The meter counts work you did. It does not predict hiring.
